items.content:
>> TrendForce: iPhone 18 Pro Costs Expected to Surge by Nearly 40%; Apple May Adjust Its Gross Margin Strategy to Stabilize Shipments

• According to TrendForce’s latest smartphone industry research, rising component prices—particularly for memory—are expected to drive up the bill of materials for Apple’s upcoming iPhone 18 series.

• TrendForce estimates that the cost of the 256GB iPhone 18 Pro will be approximately 38% higher in Q3 than that of the comparable new model launched during the same period in 2025. With memory prices expected to continue rising in 2027, the cost increase for the 256GB iPhone 18 Pro could widen further.

• Based on Apple’s recent pricing strategy for its new MacBook models, TrendForce said Apple may absorb part of the cost increase through lower gross margins, limiting price hikes for the iPhone 18 Pro series to stabilize shipments.

• TrendForce also noted that Apple may reassess the pricing of older iPhone models. It cannot rule out the possibility that Apple will raise the prices of previous-generation models alongside the launch of the new series to cushion the impact of rising memory prices.

 $AAPL

items.content:
According to Taiwanese media reports, AI demand has set off a race to raise prices and a scramble for volume in MLCCs.

Word in the industry is that some customers are offering two to three times the going price to major passive component makers such as Yageo (2327) and Murata Manufacturing just to lock down enough supply.

Yageo, for its part, acknowledged that "MLCC demand really is very strong."

Another notable shift is customers racing to lock in long term contracts.

Yageo said AI related customers are increasingly moving to secure passive component supply for the next six months, and in some cases several years out, through long term contracts in order to reduce supply chain risk.

Shipments of high specification applications such as AI servers and data centers are ramping quickly, so demand for high capacity, high reliability products is surging. Large customers generally receive higher priority in capacity allocation, while the volumes available to small and midsize customers keep shrinking. Customers with thin inventories of their own, worried that a component shortfall will disrupt shipments of their finished products, have little choice but to bid higher to secure the limited supply on offer.

items.content:
Samsung Hits 80% Yield on HBM4, Ramping Up Supply

According to Korean press reports, Samsung has lifted its HBM4 yield to 80%. In the early days of mass production this February the yield was still below 60%, so this is a remarkable improvement in just six months.

Per a source cited by Korean media, an industry official said: "The year-end yield target had originally been 80%, but as second-half production volumes ramped up in earnest, the pace of process improvement outpaced expectations."

With the HBM4 yield getting on track so quickly, Samsung has reportedly decided to raise Q3 HBM4 revenue by more than 3x quarter-on-quarter, and has set a plan to lift HBM4 to over 60% of total HBM revenue in the second half. It is also said to have set a target of raising its HBM market share by year-end to a level comparable to its DRAM market share (roughly 38%).
